institutionName: Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: To come to a city, where I could study and be close to nature at the same time.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: A bit frustrating. NTNU, KU and Erasmus will send a lot of relevant but sometimes confusing information. Tip: Read the mails twice and create an inbox just for exchange emails so they don't get lost. You get a lot of links, usernames and codes that you need at different times

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We got information emails, had a physical welcome meeting and a webpage called "NTNU GO" where there were some relevant information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: NTNU really wants to inform you, but sometimes forgets the most basic information, such as "what is a FEIDE user, when do you get your email and where do you check your course information" because there is SO much to know. Give it time and be patient :)

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
A bit challenging, but it ended up really well in the end. I started by living in a place where I was cheated by my landlord in terms of location, quality, etc. and had to move. You can find private rooms and apartments via
Finn.no
and
Hybel.no

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Many private landlords manage shared apartments, and therefore you rarely meet or read much about the people you will be living with. Ask the landlord if you can come and meet the people you will be living with before you sign a contract. And be very clear about agreeing on a notice period. Some landlords would like you to commit to six months, and I would not recommend that.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Some landlords take advantage of exchange students who do not know the city and are sometimes desperate to find a place to live. Some of my friends ended up paying overprice for simple and remote apartments and rooms of poor quality. Search for the address beforehand and find out how long it takes to walk and take the bus to »Gløshaugen» and »Studentersamfundet« (the two most central study-places in the city) The city is not so big, so it should take a maximum of 10-15 minutes to get there :)

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
I found courses via the NTNU course catalogue. Here I encountered several challenges because NNTU had not stated which academic level the courses were for, so I had to apply for approval of courses in two rounds. NTNU has subsequently added the option to their course catalogue, so that you can apply for courses that suit your academic level. 
At the same time, it took a long time before I was told that I had been accepted into the courses (2 months), which is completely normal, so again: be patient.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Email-support and sometimes you could find some information on NTNUs webpage, but it is big, deep and confusing with several dead ends.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successfull, it got both courses that I had as top priorities.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Be patient, search for many different courses, consider the exam-form of the courses, as they can be a bit weird. You can also search for the course on »
karakterweb.no
«
Here you can see the average grade and how many have passed previously, to get an idea of ​​the difficulty of the course :)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was a bit disappointed with the level. One of my subjects in particular (VL3000) moved at a very fundamental level of applying and understanding theories (such as constructivist vs. behaviorist conceptualizations) rather than discussing the theories against each other and how they can contribute to a greater understanding in interaction. It was at times far too basic, which was frustrating.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Mostly power-point lectures, sometimes with groupwork, most of the times not.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
KULT3305 Teorier om kjønn, likhet og forskjell
VL3000 Vilkår for læring i arbeidsliv og samfunn

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: KULT3305 Teorier om kjønn, likhet og forskjell was great! It presented exciting and relevant theories and understandings of gender, body and inequality such as race and orientalism.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Many apartments are heated with electric radiators, and when it gets winter it can get a bit expensive if you live in an older wooden house like it did.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and beverages = especially beer is expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Trondheim has some great student opportunities likes NTNUI (Sports organisation for students) and Studentersamfundet, which is an amazing building holding a lot of different events, parties, debates etc. The local campuses does also have organisations and student associations. Right next to the city is Bymarka, which is a lovely and peaceful forest area with lakes, hills and valleys, where you can hike, tent, go running in the summer and ski in the winter. There goes buses (18) and tram (Trikken) up there everyday.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would definitely recommend joining NTNUI. You can get a cheap membership as a half-year exchange student, where you have access to their training centers, and their various sub-organizations such as diving clubs, hiking groups. NTUI also owns several different cabins, which are located out in the mountains and forests around the city, which you as a member of NTNUI can rent very cheaply. 
I also recommend going to Bymarka, I have loved that area.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go to bymarka and see if you can finde the mooses. There are different cabins in Bymarka that sell coffee and waffles, which are incredibly cozy to go to in both summer and winter. I also recommend becoming a member of NTNUI, especially the cabin group called "Koiene" where you can go on hikes to the cabins mentioned. Here you can also join in on various volunteer activities where you help paint and work on the cabins together with other young people, and it's incredibly fun.
Different cultural activities and events can be found at
https://trdevents.no/

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, but I am danish, and I understand swedish and norwegian easily and that gave me an advantage to adjust quickly.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
Do NOT join the ESN Group (Erasmus Student Network). Their activities (such as trips to Lofoten and various parties) are presented as "once-in-a-lifetime" opportunities, but it is expensive and here you are only with other exchange students, instead of meeting local young people. 

The same goes for apartments and the room rented through the university organization (called SIT) - if you want to meet locals, you have to live with them. Otherwise it becomes a small international exchange bubble.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
Norwegians can be a little more reserved in their attitude towards new people. It's not that they don't like talking to strangers, but they just have to look someone over before they take them in. 

All shops, restaurants etc. close on Sundays, and it requires you to think ahead sometimes because nothing is open. The city can therefore also feel quite dead on Sundays if you don't make plans or enjoy a nice quiet day at home

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The nature!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be patient with NTNU 
2. Be open to the fact that your exchange may not go exactly as you planned, but that doesn't mean it wasn't a succes! 
3. Set a flexible budget. Norway is expensive on the long run.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
NTNU can be a bit chaotic and confusing with their different student accounts and webpages – Be patient<3 
It gets dark in november and december. Remember to get out and absorb some sun, when it is there.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To go on trips and hike in the mountains and forests every week and to get local friends <3

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding a good place to live.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Do it! Go to Trondheim! :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
